title: A Pikachu Plush Spent 67 Days Aboard the International Space Station
excerpt: The ESA–Pokémon partnership for World Space Week sent a spacesuited plush into orbit with astronaut Sophie Adenot; 1,040 orbits later, the tour video is out.
body:
• A Pikachu plush dressed in a custom white spacesuit spent 67 days aboard the International Space Station — from April 11 to June 17 — completing roughly 1,040 orbits alongside ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot.
  • The European Space Agency released a two-minute video this week showing Adenot giving the floating Pokémon a guided tour of the station, including the water-recycling system, scientific freezers, crew quarters and the Cupola observatory.
  • The mission is part of an official partnership between the ESA and The Pokémon Company International to mark World Space Week (October 4–10), aimed at getting children excited about space.
  • The partnership extends beyond the video: a family exhibition touring ESA sites and European museums runs through April 2027, and an Astronaut Pikachu event in Pokémon GO runs until April 30, 2027.

Astronaut Pikachu reports for duty

Pikachu is officially an astronaut. Sort of. A plush version of the Pokémon mascot, kitted out in a tiny custom spacesuit, spent 67 days aboard the International Space Station earlier this year as part of a partnership between the European Space Agency and The Pokémon Company International — and this week the ESA released video of the yellow traveller getting a private tour of the orbiting laboratory.

https://x.com/IntEngineering/status/2107878703720001600

The plush flew with French ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot during her εpsilon mission, floating about 250 miles above Earth from April 11 to June 17. The station circles the planet roughly every 90 minutes — 16 sunrises and sunsets a day — which is how a stuffed animal racked up about 1,040 orbits and roughly 28 million miles of travel in just over two months.

In the newly released two-minute video, Adenot guides the floating Pikachu through the station's systems: the water-recycling system, the scientific freezers, the crew quarters, and the Cupola, the European-built observation module where astronauts watch Earth pass beneath them.

Why ESA sent a plush to space

The trip is timed to World Space Week, the UN-declared annual celebration of space science that runs from October 4 to 10. ESA's logic is straightforward: a plush Pokémon gets children to pay attention to space in a way a press release never will.

"Inspiring future generations is a key part of ESA's mission. Through this collaboration with Pokémon, we are unlocking new ways for people across Europe to connect with space through a unique and engaging experience."

— Josef Aschbacher, ESA Director General

The partnership goes well beyond one plush and one video. A family-friendly exhibition using Pokémon-themed panels to explain how Europe launches missions, supports astronauts and studies the universe is touring ESA facilities and major science museums across Europe through April 2027. Visitors can also encounter Astronaut Pikachu in Pokémon GO, with one-star raids, timed research and venue-specific location backgrounds running from October 4, 2026 through April 30, 2027.

The humans alongside the mascot

Adenot herself had a serious mission: she has spent more than 200 days in space, conducted scientific research and completed three spacewalks over the summer to help maintain the station. The Pikachu tour footage was captured alongside that work. Expedition 75's crew also includes NASA flight engineer Anil Menon, an Indian-origin astronaut — a reminder that the station's human roster is as international as its plush one.

Outreach that works

Space agencies have long understood that mascots open doors. NASA flew everything from Lego figures to a Buzz Lightyear toy; JAXA and Roscosmos have their own traditions. ESA's bet is that Pikachu — one of the most recognised characters on the planet — can carry space science into households that would never watch a launch stream.

The early signs are encouraging: the video and the accompanying photos of Pikachu floating in the Cupola have travelled widely this week, and the museum exhibitions give the partnership a two-year shelf life well beyond the news cycle.

What's next

The Pokémon GO event and the touring exhibitions carry the partnership into 2027. And somewhere in ESA's archives now sits one of the most-travelled plush toys in history — 1,040 orbits, 67 days in microgravity, and a guided tour most humans will never get.
